summary: Specifies the steps a host takes to configure its own IPv6 addresses automatically on an interface. It lets a host form addresses without a server handing them out. It was a draft standard, replaced by RFC 4862.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer can make up its own address by combining a local street name with something unique to itself, so nobody has to hand it one.

questions: what is ipv6 stateless address autoconfiguration
how does ipv6 duplicate address detection work
how is an ipv6 link-local address formed
subtitle: How an IPv6 host builds its own addresses from a router's prefix and its own interface identifier, with no server needed.

tldr.problem: Hosts need unique, routable addresses without manual setup, and small sites should not need a server or even a router to start talking.
tldr.mechanism: A host forms a link-local address from a well-known prefix and its interface identifier, checks it is unique with Duplicate Address Detection, then combines prefixes from Router Advertisements with the same identifier to make more addresses.
tldr.outcome: This document was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 1971 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4862.

today: RFC 2462 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 1971. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 4862.

sections.title: Stateless and Stateful Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
IPv6 defines two ways for a host to get its addresses. In the stateless mechanism the host builds its own addresses from locally available information plus information advertised by routers. In the stateful mechanism the host asks a server that keeps a database of which addresses went to which hosts. The details of the stateful protocol are left to other work.

The two complement each other and may run at the same time. A host might build its own addresses statelessly but fetch other settings from a server. Stateless is used when a site does not care about exact addresses so long as they are unique and routable; stateful when the site wants tighter control. Router Advertisement messages tell hosts which to use.

The process applies only to hosts. Routers must be configured some other way, though they are expected to make link-local addresses this way and to pass Duplicate Address Detection on all addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Some kids get their locker number handed out by a teacher. Others work out their own from their class and their name. Both ways can be used together.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The design aims at five things.

  • No manual configuration of machines before they join a network.
  • Small sites on a single link work plug-and-play, with no server or router, using link-local addresses.
  • Large sites with several networks and routers need no stateful server, because routers advertise the active prefixes on each link.
  • Renumbering is graceful: addresses are leased for a time and an interface can hold several at once, so old and new prefixes work side by side during a transition.
  • Administrators can choose stateless, stateful or both, using flags in Router Advertisements.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is that you can plug in a computer and it just works, even when the school changes all its room numbers.

sections.title: How a Host Configures Itself
sections.content:
Autoconfiguration happens per interface, on multicast-capable links, when the interface is enabled. The typical steps are:

  1. Form a link-local address by appending the interface identifier to the well-known link-local prefix.
  2. Check that this tentative address is unique by sending a Neighbor Solicitation. If it is not unique, autoconfiguration stops and manual configuration is needed.
  3. Assign the address. The host now has IP connectivity with neighbors on the link.
  4. Send Router Solicitations to the all-routers multicast group, rather than wait for the next periodic Router Advertisement.
  5. Use the advertisement's flags and Prefix Information options to build global and site-local addresses, or fall back to stateful configuration.

A "managed address configuration" flag says whether to use stateful autoconfiguration for addresses, and an "other stateful configuration" flag says whether to use it for other information. A host may do link-local setup in parallel with waiting for a Router Advertisement, since a router may delay its reply for a few seconds.

Addresses go through two phases. A preferred address can be used freely. A deprecated address is discouraged for new communication but still works for existing ones. When the valid lifetime ends, the address becomes invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: First you pick a name only your street knows, and shout to check nobody else has it. Then you ask the street's helper what the full address prefix is and add your name to it.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses and Prefix Processing
sections.content:
A link-local address is the prefix FE80::0 with the interface identifier replacing its right-most N bits. If the identifier is longer than 118 bits, autoconfiguration fails. Identifiers are typically 64 bits and based on EUI-64. A link-local address has an infinite preferred and valid lifetime.

For global and site-local addresses, a host examines each Prefix Information option in a Router Advertisement. It ignores the option if the Autonomous flag is not set, if the prefix is the link-local prefix, or if the preferred lifetime exceeds the valid lifetime. Otherwise, for a new prefix with a nonzero valid lifetime, it appends its interface identifier to the prefix. If prefix length plus identifier length is not 128 bits, the option MUST be ignored.

When the prefix matches an existing autoconfigured address, the lifetime is refreshed under rules that block a denial of service: a bogus unauthenticated advertisement cannot shorten a lifetime below two hours, because legitimate periodic advertisements cancel short lifetimes before they take effect. With no routers on the link, a host MUST attempt stateful autoconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: Your address is the street prefix plus your own name. If someone shouts a fake message that the street name is about to expire, you do not believe it unless it keeps being said.

sections.title: Duplicate Address Detection
sections.content:
Before assigning a unicast address, a node performs Duplicate Address Detection whenever the interface variable DupAddrDetectTransmits is greater than zero. Its default is 1. A value of zero turns the check off. Anycast addresses MUST NOT be checked.

The node joins the all-nodes multicast address and the solicited-node multicast address of the tentative address, then sends Neighbor Solicitations with the target set to the address, the source set to the unspecified address and the destination set to the solicited-node multicast address. Messages are spaced by RetransTimer milliseconds. If it is the first message after interface initialization, the node delays a random time up to MAX_RTR_SOLICITATION_DELAY.

The address is a duplicate if a Neighbor Advertisement for it arrives, or if another node's DAD solicitation for it is seen. A tentative address MUST NOT be assigned if it is a duplicate, and the node SHOULD log a system management error. A duplicate link-local address formed from an interface identifier means the interface SHOULD be disabled. Where all addresses come from the same identifier, testing the link-local address is sufficient. The RFC notes the method is not completely reliable, for example if the link was partitioned during the check.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using a nickname, you call it out loud. If anyone answers to it, you pick another one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stateless autoconfiguration lets a host join a network and start communicating without registering or authenticating. The RFC says this threat is inherently present in the Internet architecture, since any node with a physical attachment can make an address that gives connectivity.

Duplicate Address Detection also opens a denial of service possibility: any node can answer Neighbor Solicitations for a tentative address, making the other node reject it. This is like other attacks that spoof Neighbor Discovery messages, and can be addressed by requiring that Neighbor Discovery packets be authenticated, for example with the IP Authentication Header from RFC 2402.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone standing in the schoolyard can pick a name and join in. A prankster can also pretend to own your chosen name so you have to pick again.
